name: Two-Stage Rocket
overview:
A rocket is a machine for carrying something into orbit by throwing mass out of its back very fast. Its engines burn fuel and liquid oxygen and blast the hot gas out through bell-shaped nozzles; pushing that gas backwards pushes the rocket forwards. Reaching orbit means hitting about 28,000 km/h sideways, so most of a rocket is propellant tanks.

This one has two stages. The first stage, with nine engines, lifts everything off the pad and through the thick lower atmosphere, then separates about two and a half minutes in. It flips around, relights its engines, unfolds its grid fins to steer, and lands on four legs so it can fly again. The second stage, with a single engine built for vacuum, finishes the climb to orbit.

The satellite rides on top inside the payload fairing, a nose cone in two halves that shields it from air friction and buffeting. Once the rocket is above most of the atmosphere the fairing splits open and falls away, and the satellite is later released on its own.

name: Electric Car Drive Unit
overview:
A drive unit is what an electric car has where a petrol car has its engine and gearbox. It sits between the rear wheels and turns electricity from the battery into the torque that turns them.

It has three main parts. The inverter on top takes the battery's direct current and, by switching transistors thousands of times a second, turns it into three-phase alternating current. That current flows through copper windings in the motor's stator and makes a rotating magnetic field. The rotor, studded with permanent magnets, is dragged round by that field, up to about 18,000 rpm, with no contact and almost no wear.

That speed is far too high for the wheels, so a two-stage gearbox steps it down about nine to one. The differential then lets the left and right wheels turn at different speeds through corners. There's no clutch and no gear changing: one ratio covers everything from a standing start to top speed, and when you lift off, the motor works as a generator to recharge the battery.

name: Camera Drone
overview:
A camera drone is a small flying robot built to hold a camera perfectly steady in the air. It's a quadcopter: four propellers, each on its own electric motor, provide all the lift and all the steering. There are no control surfaces; it moves by spinning some propellers faster than others.

Two propellers spin clockwise and two anticlockwise so their twisting forces cancel. To move forward, the drone speeds up its rear motors and tilts; to turn, it speeds up one diagonal pair. The flight computer makes these adjustments hundreds of times a second, using gyroscopes, accelerometers, GPS, a compass and downward cameras, so it can hover in one spot by itself.

The camera hangs under the nose on a three-axis gimbal: small motors that counter every tilt and shake of the body, so the footage stays level and smooth. A smart battery powers everything for around half an hour, and the arms fold in so the whole thing packs down to about the size of a water bottle.

name: Mechanical Watch
overview:
A mechanical watch keeps time with springs and gears and no battery. Everything is driven by one coiled mainspring. In an automatic watch like this one, a weighted rotor swings as you move your wrist and winds the spring for you; you can also wind it with the crown.

The mainspring unwinds through a gear train: a series of wheels, each turning faster than the last, that end at the escapement. On its own the spring would let go in seconds. The escapement makes it go slowly: an escape wheel is locked and released one tooth at a time by the pallet fork, which is rocked back and forth by the balance wheel. That release is the tick you hear.

The balance wheel and its hairspring are the actual timekeeper. Like a pendulum, they swing back and forth at a steady rate, here four times a second, and each swing in either direction lets the gear train advance one step: eight ticks a second. Gears off the train turn the minute hand once an hour and the hour hand once every twelve hours. Synthetic ruby jewels serve as nearly frictionless bearings.

name: Jet Engine
overview:
A jet engine makes thrust by throwing a huge amount of air backwards. This one is a high-bypass turbofan, the type on almost every airliner. It does four things in order: suck, squeeze, bang, blow.

At the front, the big fan pulls in air. Most of that air (here about ten times as much as goes through the middle) bypasses the core and is simply pushed out the back by the fan. That cool, slow bypass stream makes most of the thrust, quietly and efficiently. The rest enters the core, where the compressor's rows of spinning blades squeeze it to about thirty times atmospheric pressure.

In the combustor, fuel is sprayed into that compressed air and burned continuously. The hot, expanding gas rushes out through the turbines and spins them. The high-pressure turbine drives the compressor through one shaft, and the low-pressure turbine drives the fan through a second shaft running inside the first. Whatever energy is left leaves through the exhaust nozzle. Around it all, the nacelle smooths the airflow, and its reverser cowls can redirect the fan air forward to slow the aircraft after landing.

name: Road Bicycle
overview:
A bicycle is a machine for turning pedalling into forward motion as efficiently as possible. Your legs push the pedals round; the cranks turn the chainring, the chain carries that turn back to a sprocket on the rear wheel, and the rear wheel pushes the bike along. The ratio between the chainring and the sprocket you're in sets how far the bike travels per pedal stroke.

The frame is two triangles: the front triangle (top tube, down tube and seat tube) and the rear triangle (seat stays and chain stays). Triangles don't flex easily, so the frame stays stiff while weighing very little. The fork holds the front wheel and turns in the head tube when you steer; its angle and offset make the bike steady enough to ride no-handed.

Each wheel is a tension structure: thin spokes, pulled tight, hang the hub from the rim, so the wheel carries the rider's weight while weighing under a kilogram. Derailleurs shift the chain between sprockets for different gears, and rim brakes squeeze pads onto the wheel rims to stop.
